It may not be realistic for companies themselves to take care of it for two reasons.

First off, this would presumably be a progressive system in which a company worth a trillion dollars pays a greater proportional share than a small business with 2 employees. A cost that is completely negligible to big business would be crippling to a small business. For instance the 6 Waltons of WalMart pay themselves about $3 billion a year in dividends alone. That handout alone would be more than enough to give every one of their 1.4 million US employees more than 5 weeks paid leave every year. Also I've been somewhat conflating paid leave with medical/family leave. If we're only talking about the latter then this point becomes even more important since it basically ends up like an insurance program and insurance programs only work effectively when you have large numbers of subscribers.

Another issue is there's a big conflict of interest in having employers handle it themselves. The cost of losing a skilled employee for 5 weeks is vastly greater than the cost of 5 weeks of that employee's base salary. There would certainly be a lot of nastiness and coercion, soft and hard, that would likely take place to get people to 'voluntarily' sacrifice their leave. Soft incentives would be things like temporary 5 week raises which we could propagandize as "loyalty pay." Hard coercion might be things like reducing the evaluations of individuals in reviews or reducing/denying their pay raises if they don't sacrifice their leave. Things that would all be difficult to prove were precisely because of refusing the sacrifice their leave. Now this coercion doesn't necessarily go away putting a third party (the government in this case) in charge of it, but it helps mitigate it at least and I'm generally reluctant to avoid any scheme where you end up having the fox guarding the henhouse.

This is an argument that I have seen many times, especially when automation is brought up. It is the same arguments that was used for newsboys, farriers, milkmen, auto assemblers and and endless number of jobs that have been made obsolete by the advancement of technology. I'm sure you have heard of the Luddite fallacy and the Lump of labour fallacy (excuse the wiki links, just the most clearly written summaries, lots can be found elsewhere in more detail), these say that the labor pool and composition of the labor market are not eliminated or minimized by advancements in technology, just that they shift and adapt their compositions. This adaptation is essential to every organisms survival, and while not so much a biological adaptation, this 'workforce adaptation' is crucial in today's world. We should not simply prop up jobs that are essentially obsolete or could be done in a better, more efficient manner simply because someone screams that they don't know what to do now. If we did that, my children would not be able to take advantage of decreases in consumer prices, increases in overall quality of goods and advancements in technology that cover every sector from education to healthcare to food prep. They would grow up looking forward to working jobs that provide no advancement because we have determined to keep these old professions alive simply to provide opportunity to people that refuse to adapt. Elon Musk isn't Elon Musk because of what he would accept given to him, he is Elon Musk because of his vision, and if we had 100 Elon Musks, we wouldn't have 100 people fighting to get into the same revolutionary technology then being forced to give up and flip burgers, we would have 100 unique revolutionary technologies.

As for the cost of an MBA, the particular degree wasn't core to my argument it just related better to the path of someone in retail, and while I agree that there are institutions that you can attend that are extremely overpriced, there are also institutions that are completely affordable. It is entirely possible to attend a community college, while working full time, to achieve an associates degree in business, programming, as a foundation to an engineering degree or a number of other valuable paths and graduate without any debt with a good foot on the path to bettering one's position. I know this because I did it. I could not afford an expensive private university, so I looked at the options provided to me and chose the best option. I am not special in this regard, it is an option available to anyone if they are willing to make the sacrifices (time, discretionary spending, etc). Even if you don't want to spend the money on CC, there are an incredible number of free courses online (some provided by MIT that actually can lead to degrees) if you really want to learn. In my mind it is about personal responsibility, if you want something badly enough, you don't stop trying when something gets in your way and sit down to complain about "it's too hard, this one thing I tried didn't work, so now I need someone to do it for me and take care of me".
